0.0.n: Suggests the speaker expects this desire to remain true; it does not itself mean again.

0.1.n: Links to ワールドカップ through の to specify the upcoming tournament.

0.2.n: Connects 次 to ワールドカップ, making next World Cup.

0.3.n: The name of the international football tournament, written in katakana.

0.4.n: Marks the tournament as the setting for the match.

0.5.n: Adds the next World Cup to previous occasions of playing Spain.

0.6.n: A country name referring here to Spain's national football team.

0.7.n: Marks Spain as the other team involved in playing.

0.8.n: やる becomes やりたい to express desire; です makes the question polite.

0.9.n: Ends the sentence as a polite question.

1.0.n: Directly rejects the suggestion of wanting another match.

1.2.n: With a negative expression, indicates no further desire to do something.

1.3.n: やりたい becomes negative やりたくない; です adds politeness.

1.4.n: Softens the answer and gives it a conversational, reflective tone.

2.0.n: Read なんで here; this is a casual question asking for a reason.

3.0.n: Introduces an explanation rather than rejecting the previous question.

3.2.n: Emphasizes that the situation continues even now.

3.3.n: A casual filler used while gathering thoughts, not a specific thing.

3.4.n: A hesitation filler here, rather than pointing to a particular object.

3.6.n: Refers to the countries represented by the people talking.

3.7.n: Follows a noun to describe a relationship among members of the same category.

3.8.n: Connects 国同士 to 話, describing a discussion involving their countries.

3.9.n: Together with になる, describes what the conversation turns to.

3.10.n: Marks the topic that the conversation turns into with なる.

3.11.n: Past form of なる; before とき, it marks reaching that conversational situation.

3.12.n: Follows a description to identify the time or occasion it happens.

3.13.n: Marks とき as the occasion when the following statement applies.

4.0.n: A first-person pronoun commonly used by male speakers.

4.1.n: Combines with 僕 and としては to emphasize his personal perspective.

4.2.n: Indicates the capacity or standpoint from which he is speaking.

4.3.n: Highlights his personal standpoint, potentially contrasting it with other perspectives.

4.4.n: In マウントを取る, this slang describes asserting superiority or having bragging rights; を is omitted here.

4.5.n: The can-do form of 取る; with マウント, it means being able to assert superiority.

4.6.n: Casual contraction of ので, presenting this as his reason for avoiding another match.

5.1.n: Plural of お前; a rough, familiar address that can sound rude.

5.2.n: Casually leaves what they are saying unspecified and gives it a dismissive tone.

5.3.n: 言っている shortened to 言ってる, describing ongoing talk.

5.4.n: Contrasts their talk with the fact that they lost.

5.6.n: 負けている shortened to 負けてる; here it describes the result of the earlier match.

5.7.n: Emphasizes the loss as a fact the listener should recognize.

5.8.n: Seeks agreement; together with よ, it pointedly reminds the listener of a shared fact.

5.10.n: Casual form of という, connecting the quoted words to 話.

5.11.n: Refers to the quoted comment; the usual を before できる is omitted.

5.12.n: Expresses being able to make that kind of comment.

5.13.n: Casual contraction of ので, continuing his explanation of why he prefers not to play again.

6.0.n: Used directly as a time expression without a particle.

6.1.n: A spoken hesitation filler while he develops his explanation.

6.2.n: Plain form placed before 可能性 to describe what might happen.

6.3.n: 負ける directly modifies this noun, specifying the possible outcome.

6.4.n: Makes the chance of losing the topic of his preference.

6.5.n: Combines with でも to emphasize that even a small reduction matters.

6.6.n: After 少し, stresses that the smallest degree would still be preferable.

6.7.n: Describes the probability; the following 方 creates a comparison favoring a lower chance.

6.8.n: In adjective + 方がいい, identifies the alternative the speaker prefers.

6.9.n: Marks the lower-chance option as what is preferable.

6.10.n: With 方が, expresses a preference rather than simply calling something good.

6.11.n: Casual contraction of ので, linking this reasoning to his final conclusion.

7.0.n: Frames his decision as the current position, without committing forever.

7.1.n: With いい, signals that he has had enough and does not need another match.

7.2.n: いいです politely declines anything further here, rather than approving another match.

7.3.n: Softens his concluding statement into a relaxed conversational remark.

0.lit: After all, at the next World Cup too, do you want to play against Spain?
0.tip: たい expresses wanting to do something; と marks the opponent here.

1.lit: No, I do not want to play anymore, you know.
1.tip: To negate a wish, change たい to たくない.

2.tip: 何で is read なんで when casually asking why.

3.lit: Well, still, like, um, when it turns to discussion between countries,
3.tip: 話になる means the conversation turns to a topic.

4.lit: As for me as an individual, because I can take the upper hand.
4.tip: マウント取れる is slang for being able to assert superiority or claim bragging rights.

5.lit: Because I can make the remark, You guys are saying something, but you have lost, right?
5.tip: っていう connects the quoted taunt to 話, identifying the kind of remark he can make.

6.lit: Next time, um, as for the chance of losing, because even a little lower is better,
6.tip: Adjective + 方がいい expresses a preference: here, a lower chance is better.

7.lit: For now, I am already good, you know.
7.tip: もういいです can mean no more is needed, rather than that something is good now.
